model.label: Segmented system: employment-based social insurance institutes for formal workers, tax-funded public services for everyone else (now largely run by IMSS-Bienestar), and a large out-of-pocket private sector

overview.statement: Mexico's constitution has recognised health as a fundamental right since reforms in 1983, yet the authors of a 2025 national study judge that universal health coverage has still not been achieved, held back by fragmentation among public providers and limited public investment.

The 2020 Observatory review describes three parallel parts: social insurance tied to employment, public services for people without social insurance backed by a financial protection scheme, and a private sector of providers, insurers and suppliers.

Formal-sector workers and their families are covered by separate social security institutions: ISSSTE for state workers (13.7 million people), the IMSS for private-sector employees (68.7 million), and smaller institutes for employees of the state oil company Pemex and the armed forces.

IMSS-Bienestar, a programme created in 1973 for marginalised populations, was expanded in 2022 to serve informal workers and the unemployed in place of INSABI; by 2024 it served 50 million people in the 23 of 32 states that signed federalisation agreements, while state health services in the states that opted out served 15.6 million.
In 2018, 13.6% of the population (about 17.8 million people) had no public financial protection entitling them to free public care, and likely no private insurance either.
Coverage is unstable because it follows employment: during 2014, up to 38% of people insured by the IMSS left their jobs for more than two months and so lost access to IMSS medical facilities.
Legal eligibility for health coverage depends on a person's employment status, and differs according to whether the job is public or private and formal or informal.

financing.statement: Social insurance for formal-sector workers is financed jointly by workers, employers and the federal government; worker and employer contributions go straight to the IMSS, while the government's share comes through the federal budget.

In 2015 social insurance accounted for 30% of total health spending while covering over 42% of the population, and public services for others were paid from general taxes and government revenues; the Seguro Popular financing system made up 24% of total health spending.

Seguro Popular, started in 2003, copied the three-way funding of social insurance: the federal government paid a fixed fee per enrolled person (largely from rising oil revenue), states added half that amount, and enrollees above the poverty level were to pay an annual income-related fee.
Private insurance played a small but growing part in funding, rising from 2.3% of total health spending in 2000 to 5% in 2015.

National health accounts show government health spending for people without social security rising from 0.84% of GDP in 2003 to 1.42% in 2009, narrowing the gap with spending for people with social security (1.67% in 2009).

covered.statement: Until its abolition, Seguro Popular promised enrollees a benefit package free at the point of use; its core catalogue (CAUSES) listed 294 interventions across prevention, general and specialist medicine, emergencies, general surgery and obstetrics.

Under Seguro Popular, the package was revised every two years, and high-cost treatments for its catastrophic expenditure fund were chosen through a General Health Council consultation using criteria such as cost-effectiveness and affordability, with a technical committee deciding what to fund depending on the money available; the fund covered 66 high-cost interventions.

Medicines and devices must be registered by the General Health Council before each public institution decides whether to put them on its own approved list, based on whether it considers them necessary and affordable.

Seguro Popular paid for a defined essential package that included tertiary care and medicines, funded according to enrolment; INSABI, which replaced it, in practice covered less, excluded tertiary care, and did not clearly define its financing.
Emergency departments in both public and private hospitals take patients regardless of which institution covers them.
As of the 2020 review, long-term care was practically non-existent, palliative care policy was recent, and mental health services were underdeveloped and centred on psychiatric hospitals.
INSABI took over from Seguro Popular on 1 January 2020 with the aim of providing health services, medicines and supplies free of charge at all levels of care to people without social security.

cost_sharing.statement: Each of the public contributory schemes (IMSS, ISSSTE and other social insurance institutions, and formerly the Seguro Popular system) covers its own population and provides most services without user fees.
Seguro Popular was free for members in the lower five income deciles, which include most Mexicans, while higher-income members owed an annual contribution tied to income.
In practice most Seguro Popular members in the higher income deciles were enrolled without the contribution being collected.
People without Seguro Popular (later INSABI) cover, and even people with other insurance, can use Ministry of Health hospitals and state facilities by paying out of pocket on an income-related scale.
Medicines made up the largest share of out-of-pocket health spending among households covered by Seguro Popular/INSABI (64.5%) and households with mixed public coverage (63.6%).

The 2020 review found that long waits, lack of trust and missing medicines push many people to private providers, and that the probability of paying out of pocket is high even for people who have public insurance.
